summary: Lake Erie light at the Maumee Bay entrance on an island split between Ohio and Michigan. Its 1866 tower was lit until 1904; it is closed, on private land.

structures.note: Square brick tower of 1866 (LighthouseFriends); the US Lighthouse Society gives 1831 as the year the tower was established. See notes.
Keeper's dwelling attached to the tower; LighthouseFriends calls the lighthouse now just a shell

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds and tower closed. Best seen by boat; some summer Sunday cruises pass the island.

events.note: Government buys the island back from Edward Bissell for $300 (May 21, 1831)
Conical forty-foot tower built by contractor Philo Scovile
Station established (US Lighthouse Society)
Rise in Lake Erie cut the island from eight acres to just over an acre (LighthouseFriends)
Pile protection works under way; superintendent of public works injured by a pile driver (injury of 18 July 1837, reported by the Maumee Express of 22 July 1837)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed in the lantern room
New square brick tower of Milwaukee brick, 45 feet, funded by $12,000 from Congress
New tower first shone on September 12, 1866 (LighthouseFriends)
Concrete retaining wall after storm damage to the pile protection; storm house, storm sashes and cellar added to the dwelling
General repairs to the keeper's dwelling; hand rail put up in the tower; boathouse rebuilt, 16 by 26 feet
New winch and rollers for the boathouse; materials obtained for repairs to the boat ways
South light of the Maumee Bay range, the rear light guiding from Turtle Island, discontinued at the opening of navigation
Toledo dispatch reports the government has decided to sell the island and abandon the light
Decommissioned May 15, 1904, when Toledo Harbor Lighthouse took over the channel
Lens removed and taken to the Maumee Bay range lights; its later fate is unknown
Sold to A. H. Merrill for $1,650 on December 6, 1904
Associated Yacht Clubs of Toledo take a five-year lease; house restored and tower refinished; later abandoned as too remote
Palm Sunday tornado reportedly blew the lantern off the lighthouse
Plan to restore the light and open the island; three vacation cabins built; stop order issued for lack of a building permit
Ice floes caused substantial damage to at least one of the newer structures
Island and lighthouse acquired by a new private owner

corrections.why: The standing tower is the brick tower of 1866 that LighthouseFriends describes (square, about 45 feet, date carved over the door). The 1831 tower was conical and was replaced. The US Lighthouse Society record gives 1831 for the tower; this disagreement is for an editor to decide.

notes_for_editor: Dates disagree. Tower: the US Lighthouse Society gives 1831 as the year the tower was established and describes a square brick tower of 44.75 feet; LighthouseFriends describes the square 45-foot brick tower as the 1866 replacement, with the date carved over the door. The record's tower entry (built 1831) is proposed as a correction to 1866; the story states both. First light: the USLHS gives 1831 for the station; the record's second source (Rowlett's directory, not read for this story) gives 1832; the 1903 Toledo dispatch in the Perrysburg Journal also gives 1831, but its OCR is too damaged to quote, so it is not quoted. Most of LighthouseFriends' history (the 1836 erosion figures, the Smith plan, the 1837 Pendergrast report, Choate's family rescue, Haynes's rescue of seven, the school, the 1929 Blade recollections, the 1933 lease, the 1965 tornado, 1991, 2002, 2009 and 2022 ownership) rests on LighthouseFriends alone and is written as its account; none of it is checked against a primary report. The Light-House Board reports for 1831 to 1890 are not in our corpus (it holds 1891 to 1901 only), so the 1831 to 1866 construction and lens dates cannot be checked there. The Maumee Express (18 July 1837) names a 'Capt. Wilkinson, superintendent of public works'; the paper does not call him a keeper, and the story does not link him to the keeper Charles Wilkinson (1839). Edson and Jacobs: the archive lists Ann M. Edson and Clara Jacobs as keepers without saying how they were related to Nathan W. Edson and Samuel Jacobs; the story says so. Life-Saving Service Table 66 (1896 report) lists 'Turtle Island, Ohio' among Great Lakes places where vessels stranded in the ten years to 1896; LighthouseFriends says no shipwreck was recorded in the area during the station's 73 years. The table's column counts are too hard to read reliably from the OCR, so the story gives no counts and cites presence only; an editor should check the scan (scan page 472) before relying on the conflict. Ownership: the owners in the 1990s to 2022 are private individuals; the story does not name them, and the current owner is not named. Range: the sources give no range; the Wikipedia article's figure is not cited and range_nm is left empty. Newspapers: searches for Haynes and Choate returned nothing relevant; Ohio papers mention the island in 1837, 1866 and 1903 only. Page numbers: the 1893 entry is cited by scan page 193 (a duplicate copy is at scan page 203), and the 1894 entry by scan page 506; the printed pages are not confirmed. The roster is the USLHS roster (NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory per the roster tool); confirm each name in a primary record before publication. LighthouseFriends' variant spellings are kept in notes (Benjamin I. Woodruff, William Haynes).
